name: Dome-Barren
description: Dome-Barren is a tiny, airless body whose surface is covered in smooth, dome-shaped protrusions of varying size, from meter-scale bumps to formations several hundred meters across. These domes are not volcanic but structural, formed by the expansion of subsurface ice deposits during a warmer period in the body's history. The ice has long since sublimated, leaving hollow stone shells that give the surface a bubble-wrap texture when viewed from altitude.

With no atmosphere and negligible gravity, Dome-Barren is a place of extremes simplified to their minimum. Light and shadow, hot and cold, surface and void. The dome formations cast curved shadows that create an undulating pattern across the surface, the only visual complexity on an otherwise monotonous body. The exposed nickel-iron material in impact sites glints against the grey regolith like coins dropped on a dusty floor.

Dome-Barren is likely a captured asteroid or a fragment of a larger body, its composition and orbital characteristics suggesting an origin in the outer system. The dome formations preserve a record of the body's thermal history, from its warmer period in a closer orbit to its current cold, distant station. The hollow interiors of the larger domes maintain slightly elevated temperatures compared to the exposed surface, the stone shells providing minimal insulation.

Dome-Barren has negligible resource value and no strategic significance. It appears in navigation databases primarily as an obstacle to be avoided and in geological catalogs as an example of cryogenic expansion morphology. A single automated survey beacon marks its position. The body is occasionally proposed as a site for small-scale testing of surface construction techniques in low-gravity environments, but no such program has been funded.
